title: Sum of Subarray Ranges
description: Brute force to optimized: enumerating every subarray directly versus the monotonic stack contribution technique applied to sum(max) minus sum(min).

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums, return the SUM of all subarray ranges. The range of a subarray is the difference between its LARGEST and SMALLEST element. A subarray is a contiguous, non-empty sequence of elements.

blocks.caption: The sum of all subarray ranges equals the sum of all subarray maximums minus the sum of all subarray minimums, each computed independently via a monotonic-stack contribution technique

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of integers nums"],["Output","The sum of (max - min) over every contiguous subarray"],["Goal","Compute the total sum without explicitly enumerating every subarray, ideally in O(n)"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 1000; -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"range = max - min\" summed over EVERY subarray","This splits cleanly into two independent sums: sum of subarray MAXIMUMS minus sum of subarray MINIMUMS"],["Each of those two sums asks \"how much does each element CONTRIBUTE, across every subarray where it is the extreme?\"","The classic monotonic stack \"contribution technique\": for each element, count exactly how many subarrays it is the min (or max) of"]]}

blocks.text: Instead of computing each subarray's range individually and summing them, the total can be reframed: sum of subarray ranges = (sum of every subarray's maximum) minus (sum of every subarray's minimum), since subtraction distributes cleanly across the sum. Each of those two sums can then be computed independently using the well-known "how many subarrays is THIS element the extreme of" contribution technique.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tallying Total Height Differences Across Every Possible Team Photo Arrangement
blocks.text: Imagine every possible contiguous GROUP of people lined up for a photo, and wanting the sum of (tallest person's height minus shortest person's height) across EVERY such group. Rather than forming every group and measuring each one directly, it is equivalent (and far easier) to separately total up "how much does the TALLEST-role contribute across all groups" and "how much does the SHORTEST-role contribute across all groups," then subtract.

blocks.caption: For each element, counting how many subarrays it starts/ends within (as the guaranteed min or max) gives its total contribution directly, without enumerating those subarrays

blocks.text: Before computing each subarray's range directly (an O(n^2) enumeration), notice that the SUM over all subarrays splits cleanly into two independent "sum of extremes" problems, each solvable in O(n) using the monotonic stack contribution technique.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: sum over all subarrays of (max - min) = (sum over all subarrays of max) - (sum over all subarrays of min), since subtraction distributes across a sum.

Observation 2: For "sum of subarray minimums," each element nums[i] contributes nums[i] multiplied by EXACTLY how many subarrays it is the minimum of, since in every such subarray, nums[i] is counted as "the minimum" exactly once.

Observation 3: The number of subarrays where nums[i] is the minimum equals (i - prevLess[i]) * (nextLessOrEqual[i] - i), where prevLess[i] is the nearest index to the LEFT with a STRICTLY smaller value (or -1), and nextLessOrEqual[i] is the nearest index to the RIGHT with a value <= nums[i] (or n): the LEFT boundary can be chosen freely in (prevLess[i], i], and the RIGHT boundary in [i, nextLessOrEqual[i]), independently.

Observation 4: Both prevLess and nextLessOrEqual (and their maximum-finding mirrors) are directly computable via the SAME monotonic stack technique used throughout this category, just tracking BOUNDARY INDICES instead of resolving direct next-greater/smaller matches.

Observation 5: The asymmetric tie-breaking (strictly-less on one side, less-or-equal on the other) is essential to avoid DOUBLE-COUNTING subarrays when duplicate values are present.

This is the monotonic stack "contribution technique": compute how many subarrays each element is the extreme of, using previous-strictly-better and next-better-or-equal boundaries, then sum each element's value times its subarray count.
Directly enumerate every subarray, tracking its running minimum and maximum as it extends, and sum up each subarray's range as it is formed.

items: For each starting index i, extend the subarray one element at a time (index j from i to n-1), updating the running min and max.
Add the current subarray's range (max - min) to a running total at every extension.

codes.python:
def sub_array_ranges(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        mn = mx = nums[i]
        for j in range(i, n):                                              # extend the subarray one element at a time
            mn = min(mn, nums[j])
            mx = max(mx, nums[j])
            total += mx - mn                                              # this subarray's range, added directly
    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(sub_array_ranges([1, 3, 3]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Extending the subarray one element at a time lets the running min/max be updated incrementally (O(1) per extension), rather than rescanning the whole subarray each time.
Every subarray's range is added directly to the total the moment it is formed.

blocks.text: Correctly sums every subarray's range, since it directly and completely enumerates every possible (start, end) pair.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2), enumerating all O(n^2) subarrays, each processed in O(1) amortized (incremental min/max tracking).
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: O(n^2) does not scale well; splitting into "sum of max" minus "sum of min," each solved via the monotonic stack contribution technique, achieves O(n) total.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force enumerates every subarray explicitly. Instead, compute "sum of subarray maximums" and "sum of subarray minimums" SEPARATELY, each using the monotonic stack contribution technique: for every element, find its previous strictly-better neighbor and next better-or-equal neighbor (using monotonic stacks), multiply the resulting left-choice-count by right-choice-count to get how many subarrays it is the extreme of, and multiply by its value to get its total contribution. Subtract the two sums.

Write one shared helper, parameterized by whether "better" means bigger (for max) or smaller (for min). For each element, compute prevBoundary (previous index with a strictly better value, via a forward monotonic stack pass) and nextBoundary (next index with a better-or-equal value, via a backward monotonic stack pass). Each element's contribution is nums[i] * (i - prevBoundary[i]) * (nextBoundary[i] - i). Sum these contributions for max and for min separately, then subtract.
Compute the sum of subarray maximums and the sum of subarray minimums independently, each via the monotonic stack contribution technique, then subtract.
Dry run for nums = [1,3,3] (computing sum of subarray MINIMUMS)

codes.python:
def contribution_sum(nums, want_max):
    n = len(nums)
    better = (lambda a, b: a > b) if want_max else (lambda a, b: a < b)     # "better" = bigger for max, smaller for min
    prev_boundary = [-1] * n                                                # previous index with a STRICTLY better value
    next_boundary = [n] * n                                                 # next index with a better-OR-EQUAL value
    stack = []
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and not better(nums[stack[-1]], nums[i]):              # pop everything NOT strictly better than nums[i]
            stack.pop()
        prev_boundary[i] = stack[-1] if stack else -1
        stack.append(i)
    stack = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        while stack and better(nums[i], nums[stack[-1]]):                  # pop everything STRICTLY worse than nums[i] (ties stay, giving <=)
            stack.pop()
        next_boundary[i] = stack[-1] if stack else n
        stack.append(i)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        left = i - prev_boundary[i]                                        # choices for the subarray's LEFT edge
        right = next_boundary[i] - i                                       # choices for the subarray's RIGHT edge
        total += nums[i] * left * right                                    # nums[i] is the extreme in exactly left*right subarrays
    return total

def sub_array_ranges(nums):
    return contribution_sum(nums, True) - contribution_sum(nums, False)    # sum(max) - sum(min) over ALL subarrays


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(sub_array_ranges([1, 3, 3]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since each of the four monotonic stack passes (prev/next boundaries, for both max and min) is a single linear scan.
Space: O(n), for the stacks and boundary arrays.

For a fixed element at index i to be the MINIMUM of a subarray, that subarray's left edge must fall somewhere strictly after the nearest smaller element to the left (otherwise that smaller element would be included, becoming the true minimum instead), and its right edge must fall somewhere before or at the nearest value <= nums[i] to the right. Multiplying the number of valid left-edge choices by the number of valid right-edge choices gives exactly the count of subarrays where nums[i] is the minimum, and each contributes nums[i] to the total sum of minimums. Using STRICT inequality on one side and NON-STRICT on the other prevents duplicate values from being double-counted across different "minimum" claims.

items: A single shared contributionSum helper, parameterized by "wantMax," avoids duplicating the boundary-finding logic for both the max and min computations.
The forward pass computes prevBoundary using a monotonic stack that pops while NOT strictly better (ensuring what remains IS strictly better, or the stack is empty).
The backward pass computes nextBoundary using a monotonic stack that pops while STRICTLY worse (allowing ties to remain, giving the "or equal" boundary).

blocks.text: "Sum of X over all subarrays" problems, where X is an extreme value (min or max), can almost always be solved with the monotonic stack contribution technique: compute, for each element, exactly how many subarrays it is the extreme of, using previous-strictly-better and next-better-or-equal boundaries.

items: Using the SAME tie-breaking rule (both strict, or both non-strict) on both sides, which would double-count (or under-count) subarrays containing duplicate values.
Forgetting that "sum of ranges" splits into "sum of max minus sum of min," and instead trying to compute the range contribution directly (which does not decompose as cleanly).
Using int instead of a wider type (long/long long) for the running totals, risking overflow given the problem's constraints on value magnitude and array length.

items: Explicitly stating "range = max - min, so the total sum splits into sum(max) - sum(min)" up front is the key reframing that makes this problem tractable, before diving into the monotonic stack mechanics.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Sum of [min/max/range] over ALL subarrays" points toward the monotonic stack contribution technique: count how many subarrays each element is the extreme of.

items: How does this problem directly build on Sum of Subarray Minimums? It computes that exact same sum (via the identical technique), plus its mirror-image "sum of subarray maximums," then subtracts them.

Why is the asymmetric tie-breaking (strict on one side, non-strict on the other) necessary? Without it, a subarray containing multiple copies of the minimum (or maximum) value could be counted as having MULTIPLE different "minimum-contributing" elements, inflating the total.

How would you adapt this to also handle a weighted variant, where each subarray's range is multiplied by its length? The same contribution technique still applies, but the per-subarray "weight" would need to be incorporated into the left*right count formula rather than a simple count.

A direct combination of the "sum of subarray minimums" and "sum of subarray maximums" monotonic stack contribution technique (Sum of Subarray Minimums, elsewhere in this category, is exactly one half of this same computation).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (monotonic stack contribution technique): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic stack contribution technique, applied twice (sum of maximums minus sum of minimums)

Core Idea: Sum of subarray ranges = sum(subarray max) - sum(subarray min); each of those sums is computed by counting, per element, exactly how many subarrays it is the extreme of, via previous-strictly-better and next-better-or-equal boundaries
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Range decomposes cleanly into max minus min, letting two independent, well-known contribution-technique sub-problems replace one harder combined problem
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: sum(range) = sum(max) - sum(min); each via nums[i] * (i - prevBetter[i]) * (nextBetterEq[i] - i)
